headline: Singapore's chip case: four people and four firms charged. No Malaysian operator publicly charged.
context: Singapore charged three men in Feb 2025 over servers its Home Affairs Minister linked to Nvidia chips sent to Malaysia; a fourth person and four firms followed by July 2026. Malaysia put US AI chips under a permit on 14 July 2025. No Malaysian operator has been publicly charged.

cards.big: Singapore's chip case grew to four people and four companies charged: three men on 27 Feb 2025, a fourth person on 2 April 2026, the firms on 1 July 2026.
cards.sub: Singapore's Minister Shanmugam said the servers possibly carried Nvidia chips and moved to Malaysia; the final destination was unknown.

cards.big: The US 'Tier 2' label came from a rule that never named Malaysia. BIS's 13 May 2025 release, as now published, cites diversion via Malaysia and Thailand.
cards.sub: BIS halted enforcement of the rule on 13 May 2025, before compliance began. GAO ruled in May 2026 that it stands until formally rescinded.

cards.big: A US indictment alleges a California firm got over US$176 million from two Malaysia-based shipment companies in 2024, in a scheme routing servers to China.
cards.sub: The US Justice Department announced the owner's arrest on 1 October 2026. The charges are allegations; no Malaysian company was charged.

cards.big: Malaysia made US-origin AI chips subject to a Strategic Trade Permit on 14 July 2025. Before that, MITI said the chips were not on the Strategic Items List.
cards.sub: Penalties under the July 2025 directive reach RM10M (RM20M with knowledge). No Malaysian operator has been publicly charged.

cards.big: Singapore prosecutes fraud on suppliers; the US prosecutes the exporter. Twenty months after the first Singapore charges, no Malaysian operator has been publicly charged.
Like writing the building code after the towers go up. Now everyone watches which ones get inspected.
cards.sub: Malaysia wrote its US-chip permit roughly five months after the Singapore charges.

cards.big: Singapore charged four people, then four companies. Malaysia wrote a permit. Twenty months on, no Malaysian operator has been publicly charged.
